## The problem

A large inflated flexible ring (tens of metres across) holds a seaweed
cultivation platform a few metres below the sea surface. Under wave and
current loading it oscillates and can tilt or fold; the ring's bending
stiffness is low and adding mass is undesirable. Want approaches to keep
the platform stable and near-horizontal that don't rely on making the
ring heavier or stiffer.

## Brief on the foreign seed: Salivary Gland Tumors Diagnosis and Treatment (Health Sciences > Medicine > Surgery > Salivary Gland Tumors Diagnosis and Treatment)

# Salivary Gland Tumors: Diagnosis and Treatment — Technical Brief

Salivary gland neoplasms are pathologically heterogeneous (>20 WHO-recognized entities) but clinical management converges on a small set of recurring mechanisms and techniques: cytologic risk stratification, fusion-gene-driven molecular diagnosis, histologic grading, and margin/nerve-sparing surgical and radiotherapeutic decision-making.

1. **Milan System for Reporting Salivary Gland Cytopathology (MSRSGC)** — Fine-needle aspiration cytology is triaged into six categories (I: non-diagnostic, II: non-neoplastic, III: AUS, IVa: benign neoplasm, IVb: SUMP, V: suspicious for malignancy, VI: malignant), each carrying an empirically derived risk of malignancy (ROM). This lets the surgeon convert a cytologic read directly into a management pathway (observation vs. core biopsy vs. resection extent) without waiting for frozen section. Standard form: category-specific ROM ranges (e.g., ~5% for II, 60–90% for V, >90% for VI), reported per institution and used to set the threshold for proceeding to surgery.

2. **Recurrent fusion oncogenes as lineage- and entity-defining drivers** — Several salivary carcinomas are chromosomal-translocation diseases: *CRTC1(MECT1)–MAML2* in mucoepidermoid carcinoma (t(11;19)) constitutively activates Notch/CREB transcriptional output; *MYB–NFIB* (or *MYBL1–NFIB*) in adenoid cystic carcinoma dysregulates a MYB transcriptional program; *ETV6–NTRK3* in mammary analogue secretory carcinoma creates a constitutively active NTRK3 tyrosine kinase. These are detected by FISH break-apart probes or RT-PCR/NGS fusion panels and are used both diagnostically (distinguishing morphologic mimics) and, for *ETV6–NTRK3*, therapeutically (predicts response to TRK inhibitors).

3. **Perineural invasion / neurotropism in adenoid cystic carcinoma** — ACC preferentially tracks along nerve sheaths (perineural and, less often, intraneural spread), driven by tumor–nerve paracrine signaling (e.g., NGF/TrkA, GDNF/RET axes) that allows tumor cells to migrate substantial distances from the visible mass along named nerves (e.g., facial, lingual, inferior alveolar). This produces skip lesions beyond grossly clear margins, is a major cause of "positive margin despite adequate resection," and is the single strongest indication for postoperative radiotherapy to the nerve tract even after complete gross excision.

4. **Histologic grading of mucoepidermoid carcinoma (AFIP/modified Goode system)** — A point-based score assigns weighted points for cystic component <20% (2 pts), neural invasion (2), necrosis (3), mitoses ≥4/10 hpf (3), and anaplasia (4); points sum to a grade (low ≤4, intermediate 5–6, high ≥7). Grade correlates with 5-year survival (>90% low-grade vs. ~25–40% high-grade) and is the primary determinant of whether elective neck dissection and adjuvant radiotherapy are added to resection.

5. **Capsular pseudopodia and tumor spillage in pleomorphic adenoma** — The pseudocapsule of pleomorphic adenoma is frequently incomplete, with finger-like tumor extensions (pseudopodia) penetrating it; simple enucleation transects these extensions and seeds the field, producing multifocal recurrence years to decades later (recurrence risk with enucleation alone can exceed 20–45% vs. <2% with a margin of normal tissue). This mechanistic fact is why extracapsular dissection or superficial/partial parotidectomy with a cuff of normal parenchyma has replaced enucleation as the surgical standard, balanced against facial nerve preservation.

6. **Facial-nerve-sparing dissection using intraoperative nerve monitoring** — Because major salivary neoplasms (especially parotid) sit against or within the facial nerve plexus, resection proceeds via nerve identification (main trunk or retrograde branch approach) with continuous electromyographic monitoring (train-of-four/free-run EMG) that signals mechanical or thermal irritation before transection. The trade-off managed is oncologic completeness (wider margin, lower local recurrence) versus nerve morbidity (facial paresis/paralysis); monitoring shifts this trade-off favorably without changing the resection plane itself.

7. **Postoperative radiotherapy (PORT) indication and dosing** — PORT is added based on a composite risk score (high-grade histology, close/positive margins, perineural or lymphovascular invasion, T3–T4 stage, nodal disease, bone invasion), since these features predict local failure with surgery alone. Standard dosing is ~60–66 Gy in 2 Gy fractions to the tumor bed/nerve tract (with a boost to gross residual disease), or fast-neutron therapy at specialized centers for unresectable/recurrent ACC given its relative radioresistance to photons; the procedural logic is a linear accumulation of risk factors that crosses a threshold triggering adjuvant treatment rather than a single deterministic indication.

proposal:
## 1. Abstract the problem

A closed loop of compliant material (near-zero bending stiffness by design, can't gain mass or stiffness) floats near a free surface and is hit by a spatially- and temporally-varying disturbance field (waves, current). The loop has to stay close to a reference shape (flat, horizontal, unfolded) despite that disturbance. Because bending stiffness is deliberately low, a local push at one point of the loop is *not* resisted locally — it has to be dealt with by something other than elastic resistance, or it will travel. The two things actually available to work with are: (a) how energy put into the loop at one point gets removed or redistributed before it turns into large-amplitude tilt/fold elsewhere, and (b) how the system decides *when and where* to intervene given only partial, noisy information about the disturbance. What's been tried and excluded: brute-force resistance (more EI, more mass) — off the table by the problem statement. The real bottleneck is a propagation/allocation problem, not a material-strength problem: energy in, undamped, on a low-stiffness closed ring goes somewhere.

## 2. Map

Going mechanism by mechanism against that abstract propagation/allocation problem:

| # | Mechanism | Addresses the abstract problem? | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Milan cytology triage (cheap first pass → escalate only if ambiguous) | Yes, as a *sensing/decision economy* pattern | Keep, secondary |
| 2 | Fusion oncogenes as lineage drivers | No — this is molecular identity typing with a therapeutic payload (kinase inhibitors) that has no physical analogue here; correspondence would be "identify which failure mode is present," which is trivially already what any vibration engineer does | Discard |
| 3 | Perineural invasion — disease spreads invisibly along a conduit beyond the visible lesion; the fix is to treat the *whole conduit*, not just the resection bed | Yes, directly — it's a statement about how local damage propagates along a low-resistance pathway beyond the point of insult | **Keep, primary** |
| 4/7 | Composite point-scored grading (Goode/AFIP) and composite-risk PORT threshold — several weak indicators summed, escalate treatment only past a threshold | Yes, as a *control-law shape* (staged/threshold response instead of continuous max effort) | Keep, secondary |
| 5 | Pseudopodia / enucleation margin | Only a vague "leave extra margin" image, no mechanism translatable into a quantity — discard as decorative | Discard |
| 6 | EMG-monitored nerve-sparing dissection | Same underlying mechanism as 4/7 (real-time signal triggers intervention before damage) — folds into that entry, adds nothing new | Merge into 4/7 |

Explicit correspondence table for the two survivors:

**Mechanism A (perineural spread → whole-tract treatment)**

| Seed element | Ring element |
|---|---|
| Tumor cells migrating along nerve sheath beyond gross margin | Flexural/bending disturbance propagating along the ring's compliant material beyond the point of wave impact |
| "Positive margin despite adequate resection" | Fold/tilt appearing at a point *other* than where the load was measured/reinforced |
| PORT applied to the entire nerve tract, not just the tumor bed | Damping applied around the entire ring circumference, not concentrated at the measured load hot-spot |
| Radiotherapy is a broadly-applicable, low-marginal-cost-per-unit-length treatment | Distributed drag/damping devices must be cheap-per-unit-length and near-zero-mass to satisfy the same "treat everywhere" strategy |

**Mechanism B (graded/threshold treatment escalation, with cheap triage)**

| Seed element | Ring element |
|---|---|
| MSRSGC categories I–VI, ROM per category | Composite instability score computed from cheap sensors |
| AUS/SUMP "indeterminate" category → order more tissue before deciding | Ambiguous mid-range score → activate denser local sensing before acting |
| Goode/AFIP weighted point sum crossing a grade boundary | Weighted sum of curvature, tilt-rate, tension asymmetry crossing an action threshold |
| PORT triggered only once composite risk crosses threshold, not for every lesion | Active ballast redistribution triggered only once composite score crosses threshold, not run continuously |

## 3. Re-instantiate

**Mechanism A — circumferential damping sized to disturbance decay length ("treat the whole tract").**

Model the ring as a closed compliant loop of bending stiffness EI (deliberately small), mass/length m, floating with distributed buoyancy stiffness k (restoring force per unit deflection from waterplane area / inflation pressure), damping/length c(s), under distributed wave loading q(s,t) around arclength s (periodic in s, period = ring circumference L):

m·∂²w/∂t² + c(s)·∂w/∂t + EI·∂⁴w/∂s⁴ − k·w = q(s,t)

Because EI is small, the EI∂⁴w/∂s⁴ term is nearly irrelevant to how a disturbance spreads — the response to a local impulsive load is governed almost entirely by k (which sets a local restoring rate) and c(s) (which sets how fast that local response decays before it can couple into neighboring arcs and build a standing pattern around the closed loop). This is exactly the perineural-invasion logic: the "visible lesion" (measured wave hot-spot) is not where the failure ultimately shows up; what matters is whether the disturbance decays before it completes a trip around the "conduit" (here, literally the ring) and reinforces itself into a fold or a rocking mode.

Design rule: choose distributed damping c(s) — deliberately *not* concentrated at the point of peak measured load — such that the decay length λ = f(k, c, m) satisfies λ < L / n for the lowest problematic circumferential mode number n (n=1 tilt, n=2 saddle/fold, etc.), so energy dissipates before it can organize into a global mode. This gives a concrete sizing target for hardware, not a hand-wave: run the equation above with a target n (say the fold mode you're most worried about) and solve for the minimum c(s) that pushes λ under L/n.

Practical zero-mass-added devices to realize c(s), spaced uniformly around the full circumference (not clustered at instrumented hot-spots): thin perforated fabric skirts hanging below the ring that generate viscous drag only under *relative* motion (no static load, negligible mass since not load-bearing); small paired ballast pockets connected by a bleed orifice so water sloshes with a phase lag and dissipates energy (a distributed tuned-liquid-column damper using ballast that's already there for buoyancy trim, not added mass); hinged flap fins that convert local relative velocity into hydraulic damping-cylinder heat. All of these add drag/damping, not stiffness or net mass — matching the constraint.

**Mechanism B — two-tier triage sensing with threshold-scheduled active response (secondary, supporting layer).**

Instrument the ring with a sparse first tier of cheap sensors (inclinometers or mooring-line tension gauges at, say, 8–16 points) — the FNA-equivalent. Compute a weighted composite instability score each cycle:

S(t) = w1·(peak local curvature) + w2·(tilt differential between opposing arcs) + w3·(tilt rate) + w4·(mooring tension asymmetry)

with weights fit the way Goode-grading weights were fit empirically (against a hydroelastic model or scaled tank data, not first-principles). Stage the response the way grade/PORT staging works:

- Low S → passive damping (Mechanism A) only, no action.
- Mid/ambiguous S (the AUS/SUMP band) → don't act yet; escalate to a denser local sensor array on that arc to determine whether it's a transient wave group (ignore) or a persistent forcing shift such as a current change (act).
- High S → active response: redistribute existing ballast water circumferentially (pump between compartments, total mass constant) to counter the specific tilt/fold mode detected, engaged only past threshold rather than run continuously.

The novel piece here — versus a generic continuous feedback controller a controls engineer would reach for anyway — is the deliberate indeterminate tier that orders more (cheap, local) data before committing an actuator, taken directly from Milan's AUS/SUMP logic.

## 4. Critique

**What's lost in translation.** Perineural spread is a *directed*, biologically gradient-driven migration along a specific, identifiable, discrete conduit (a named nerve with a known route); the ring's "conduit" is an undifferentiated continuum, and mechanical energy spreads symmetrically outward in both directions from a disturbance, with no chemotactic bias. So the seed only licenses the coarse conclusion "don't stop at the load point, treat the loop" — it gives no guidance on asymmetric allocation, and importing more of the medical picture than that (e.g., trying to find a ring equivalent of "which specific nerve branch") would be over-fitting a biological detail onto a symmetric physical system.

**Assumption that breaks.** In oncology, radiotherapy to the whole nerve tract is cheap and low-marginal-cost per unit length relative to the stakes, so "treat everywhere along the conduit" is close to a free lunch. On the ring, every meter of circumferential damping hardware costs money, adds failure points, and — even at "near-zero" individual mass — sums to a real mass/cost budget once applied around tens of metres of loop. The oncology mechanism doesn't have to justify its own marginal cost the way this transfer does; that's the single biggest place the analogy is asymmetric and could mislead a design that just says "damp everywhere, it worked for nerves."

**Second assumption that breaks.** Grade/risk-score thresholds in the Goode/PORT systems are calibrated on large multi-institutional outcome datasets. There's no equivalent population of ring failures to fit w1..w4 against; those weights would have to come from a validated hydroelastic model or physical model testing before the composite score means anything, which is a real up-front cost the medical version doesn't pay (the calibration data already exists there).

**Cheapest test.** Don't build a skirt-damper prototype first. Run the beam(-ish)-on-elastic-foundation equation above numerically (a day of work): fix a small EI representative of the actual inflated ring, sweep distributed damping density c(s) (uniform vs. clustered-at-hotspot for comparison), apply an impulsive local load, and measure whether the resulting decay length λ can be pushed below L/2 (kill the n=1 tilt mode) or L/3 (kill the n=2 fold mode) using a damping-device mass/drag budget consistent with "no added mass." If clustered damping performs almost as well as uniform circumferential damping in this model, the core claim — that low-EI rings need whole-loop treatment rather than local reinforcement — is falsified, and the transfer was decorative rather than real.
